parole.significato: Added to nouns to form masculine nouns denoting action/process, systems, philosophies, principles, doctrines, ideologie…
parole.testo: Not a native Latvian suffix, -isms occurred in many borrowings and is now fully integrated. Ultimately from Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós), like its English cognate -ism (see etymology of -ism).

parole.significato: Added to nouns to form masculine nouns denoting members/followers of a principle, religion, philosophy, lifestyle, or s…
parole.testo: Not a native Latvian suffix, -ists occurred in many borrowings and is now fully integrated. Ultimately from Ancient Greek -ιστής (-istḗs), like its English cognate -ist (see etymology of -ist).

parole.significato: Not, not having, without, opposite of.
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-) (ἀν- (an-) immediately preceding a vowel).

parole.significato: actinium (a metallic chemical element with atomic number 89.)
parole.testo: Through a European language, from Ancient Greek ἀκτίς (aktís), ἀκτῖν- (aktîn-, “ray”), because of its radiation.

parole.significato: acoustics (branch of physics that studies sounds and their properties)
parole.testo: Via some European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός (akoustikós), from ἀκούω (akoúō, “to hear”).

parole.significato: an Albanian, an Albanian man, a man born in Albania
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀλβανοί (Albanoí, “a southern Illyrian tribe”).

parole.significato: allele (one of several forms of a gene, occurring in the same position within a chromosome)
parole.testo: Originally a shortened form (cf. English allele, from allelomorph), ultimately from the Ancient Greek prefix άλληλ-, from ἄλλος (állos, “other”).

parole.significato: amethyst
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀμέθυστος (améthustos, “not drunk”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μεθύω (methúō, “I am drunk”), from μέθυ (méthu, “wine”).

parole.significato: amphitheatre
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron, “a place for viewing on both sides”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see", "to watch", "to observe”).

parole.significato: amphibian (vertebrates of the class Amphibia that live both on land and in water)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιον (amphíbion), from ἀμφί (amphí, “of both kinds”) and βίος (bíos, “life”).

parole.significato: amorphous (having a non-crystalline structure; with atoms and molecules chaotically distributed)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄμορφος (ámorphos, “without form, shapeless, deformed”), itself from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”).

parole.significato: anarchy
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía).

parole.significato: anecdote
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ἀνέκδοτος (anékdotos).

parole.significato: Antarctic (relating to, or typical of, Antarctica)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós), from ἀντί (antí, “opposite, against”) and ἄρκτος (árktos, “Great Bear; North”).

parole.significato: antonym (one of two or more linguistic elements with opposed meanings)
parole.testo: A modern coinage, meant to be the opposite of sinonīms, with components derived from Ancient Greek ἀντί (antí, “against”) and ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”), with variants that arose in various European languages around 1850-1870. It was borrowed into Latvian and made into a masculine first-declension noun (

parole.significato: anthropology (science that studies the humanity, human beings, and human societies)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man, mankind, human, humanity”) and λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”) + -ija.

parole.significato: aorta (the main artery of the circulatory system, responsible for carrying the blood from the heart to the rest of the…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ, “the arteries springing from the heart”), from ἀορτέω (aortéō), lengthened form of ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, raise”).

parole.significato: apathy (mental condition characterized by lack of will, activity, interest; indifference)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia, “impassibility”, “insensibility”, “freedom from emotion”), from ἀπαθής (apathḗs, “not suffering or having suffered”, “without experience of”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + πάθος (páthos, “anything that befalls one”,

parole.significato: argon (gaseous chemical element, an inert noble gas, with atomic number 18)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀργόν (argón), neuter of ἀργός (argós, “idle, lazy”), because of its inertness.

parole.significato: archaeology (science that studies the pasts of human societies through their material remains)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀρχαιολογία (arkhaiología, “antiquarian lore, ancient legends, history”), from ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos, “primal, old, ancient”) and λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”). It contains the suffix -ija.

parole.significato: architect
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”).

parole.significato: aristocracy
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā), from ἄριστος (áristos, “the best”) + κράτος (krátos, “rule, strength”).

parole.significato: arithmetic (branch of mathematics that studies numbers and their operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, div…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητική (τέχνη) (arithmētikḗ (tékhnē), “(art of) counting”), feminine of ἀριθμητικός (arithmētikós, “arithmetical”), from ἀριθμός (arithmós, “number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ri-dʰh₁-mó-s, form of *h₂rey- (“to cou

parole.significato: arithmetic (typical of, or associated with, arithmetic)
parole.testo: From aritmētika (“arithmetic”) + -isks. Probably not formed as such in Latvian, but borrowed and adapted from other European languages. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητική (τέχνη) (arithmētikḗ (tékhnē), “(art of) counting”), feminine of ἀριθμητικός (arithmētikós, “arithmetical”), from ἀριθμός (

parole.significato: Arctic (relating to, or typical of, the Earth's northern polar region)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikós, “of the bear, northern”), a reference to the northerly constellation Ursa Major, from ἄρκτος (árktos, “bear”).

parole.significato: an Armenian man, a man born in Armenia or of Armenian descent
parole.testo: Probably via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀρμένιος (Arménios), from Ἀρμενία (Armenía) (early 5th century BC), from Old Persian 𐎠𐎼𐎷𐎡𐎴 (a-r-mi-i-n /⁠Armina⁠/) (late 6th century BC) (q.v.).

parole.significato: asymmetry
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀσυμμετρία (asummetría).

parole.significato: astatine (nonmetallic, sometimes considered metalloid, chemical element, with atomic number 85.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄστατος (ástatos, “unstable”).

parole.significato: asteroid (celestial body smaller than a planet that orbits a star, especially the Sun)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀστεροειδής (asteroeidḗs), from ἀστήρ (astḗr, “star”) + εἶδος (eîdos, “form”).

parole.significato: athlete
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs), from ἀθλέω (athléō, “compete for a prize”), from ἆθλον (âthlon, “prize”) or ἆθλος (âthlos, “competition”).

parole.significato: bromine (nonmetallic chemical element, with atomic number 35.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek βρῶμος (brômos, “stink”).

parole.significato: barium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 56.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek βαρύς (barús, “heavy”).

parole.significato: a bible, a copy of the Bible
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek βιβλία (biblía, “books”), plural of βιβλίον (biblíon, “small book”), originally a diminutive of βίβλος (bíblos, “book”), from βύβλος (búblos, “papyrus”) (from the ancient Phoenician city of Byblos which exported this writing material).

parole.significato: democracy (form of government where the power belongs to the people)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek δημοκρατία (dēmokratía), from δῆμος (dêmos, “common people”) + κράτος (krátos, “rule, strength”).

parole.significato: diphthong (sequence of two different vowels pronounced in one syllable)
parole.testo: A borrowing, via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek δίφθογγος (díphthongos, “two sounds”), from δίς (dís, “twice”) and φθόγγος (phthóngos, “sound”).

parole.significato: dynasty (series of rulers of one family)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía, “power, dominion”).

parole.significato: dysprosium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 66.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δυσπρόσιτος (dusprósitos, “hard to get”).

parole.significato: ecology (system of interrelations between living organisms and their environment)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) and λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”) + -ija.

parole.significato: exotic
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, “foreign”, literally “from the outside”), from ἐξω- (exō-, “outside”), from ἐξ (ex, “out of”). With -isks ending.

parole.significato: energy
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἐνέργειᾰ (enérgeiă).

parole.significato: epistemology (branch of philosophy that studies knowledge, its possibility and conditions)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἐπιστήμη (epistḗmē, “science, knowledge”), from ἐπίσταμαι (epístamai, “I know”) and λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”) + -ija.

parole.significato: epithet (a term that describes or characterizes figuratively a property of an entity, phenomenon or concept; an artisti…
parole.testo: Via other European languages (e.g., French épithète), ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton, “adjective”), the neuter of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “attributed, added”), from ἐπιτιθέναι (epitithénai, “to add on”).

parole.significato: aesthetics (philosophical discipline that studies beauty, art, and creative work)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek αἰσθητικός (aisthētikós, “of sense perception”), from αἰσθάνομαι (aisthánomai, “I feel”).

parole.significato: ethnography (branch of anthropology that describes specific human peoples, cultures, and societies)
parole.testo: A new coinage, via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἔθνος (éthnos, “a people, nation”) and γράφω (gráphō, “I write”) + -ija.

parole.significato: ethnology (science that studies peoples and their cultures from a comparative and historical perspective)
parole.testo: A new coinage, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἔθνος (éthnos, “a people, nation”) and λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”) + -ija.

parole.significato: pharaoh (a supreme ruler in Ancient Egypt)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek Φαραώ (Pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ (“palace, pharaoh”, literally “pr (“house”) + ꜥꜣ (“great, big”)”).

parole.significato: philology, language and literature studies
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek φιλολογία (philología, “love of argument or reasoning, love of learning and literature”), from φίλος (phílos, “loved, beloved, dear, friend”) and λόγος (lógos, “word; treaty; study of”) with the suffix -ία (-ía) (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: physics (science that studies the general properties of matter and the laws of motion)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós, “natural”).

parole.significato: phonology (science that studies how sounds function in languages; also specifically the study of the sound structure of…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, treatise”) + -ija).

parole.significato: to photograph, to take a photograph, a picture (to capture an image with a photographic camera)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately a modern coinage based on Ancient Greek φῶς (phôs, “light”) (combining form φωτ- (phōt-)) and γράφω (gráphō, “to scratch, to scrape, to graze; to write”).

parole.significato: photographer (man who takes photographs, typically as an occupation; a specialist in photography)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately a modern coinage based on Ancient Greek φῶς (phôs, “light”) (combining form φωτ- (phōt-)) and γράφω (gráphō, “to scratch, to scrape, to graze; to write”).

parole.significato: giant (object, animal or person of unusually large size)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”), genitive form γιγάντος (gigántos), the name of a mythical race of large human-like beings. The word was apparently taken into Ancient Greek from a non-Indo-European pre-Greek language.

parole.significato: chlorine (gaseous chemical element, very toxic, with atomic number 17)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “pale green”), via English chlorine, coined by sir Humphry Davy in 1810.

parole.significato: homo- (same)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ὁμός (homós, “one and the same, common, joint”).; found only in words borrowed from other languages (compare English, German, Spanish, French, Portuguese homo-, Italian omo-).

parole.significato: hormone
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὁρμή (hormḗ, “rapid motion forwards, onrush, onset, assault, impulse to do a thing, effort”), whence ὁρμάω (hormáō, “to set in motion, urge on”).

parole.significato: idiocy (severe mental retardation)
parole.testo: Probably from Ancient Greek ἰδιωτεία (idiōteía), via some other European language.

parole.significato: idiot (person with extremely serious problems in their mental development)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “a private citizen, one who has no professional knowledge, layman”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private”); ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs) was used derisively in ancient Athens to refer to one who declined to

parole.significato: iridium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 77.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris, “rainbow”), because of the bright colour of many iridium salts.

parole.significato: iodine (nonmetallic chemical element, with atomic number 53.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἰοειδής (ioeidḗs, “violet”).

parole.significato: cadmium (metallic chemical element, quite poisonous, with atomic number 48.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek Καδμεία (Kadmeía) (calamine), a Cadmium-bearing mixture of minerals, which was named after the god Κάδμος (Kádmos) (Cadmus).

parole.significato: calligraphy, penmanship (the practice of handwriting in a beautiful, decorative style; words written in such a style)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek καλλιγραφία (kalligraphía, “pretty writing”), from κάλλος (kállos, “beauty”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to draw”), adapted to Latvian lexical patterns ( + -ija).

parole.significato: calligrapher (a man who practices calligraphy)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek καλλιγράφος (kalligráphos, “calligrapher”), from κάλλος (kállos, “beauty”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to draw”), made into a first-declension masculine noun (ending -s).

parole.significato: cardiology (branch of medicine that studies the heart, its diseases, treatments, and prevention)
parole.testo: A new coinage, ultimately from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía, “heart”) and -λογία (-logía, “study”), probably borrowed from other European languages and adapted into Latvian (e.g., + -ija).

parole.significato: clitoris (female organ of sexual stimulation, situated on the upper part of the labia majora)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís), a diminutive of uncertain origin, probably from κλείω (kleíō, “I sheathe, shut”), in reference to its being covered by the labia minora.

parole.significato: cosmos, universe, outer space (interplanetary, interstellar, intergalactic space, together with the objects found in it)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “order; world; universe”), probably via some other European language.

parole.significato: krypton (gaseous chemical element, with atomic number 36.)
parole.testo: From the neuter form of Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”).

parole.significato: Christadelphian
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós) 'Christ' + ἀδελφός (adelphós) 'brother'; probably borrowed via some other European language.

parole.significato: xenon (gaseous chemical element, with atomic number 54.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξένον (xénon), neuter of ξένος (xénos, “foreign, strange”).

parole.significato: lanthanum (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 57.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek λανθάνω (lanthánō, “escape notice”), because it had gone long undetected in mineral ores.

parole.significato: logic
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from feminine of λογικός (logikós, “of or pertaining to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”).

parole.significato: mega-
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “great, large, mighty”).

parole.significato: metropolis (the mother city or country of a colony)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis, “mother city”), from μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”) + πόλις (pólis, “city (state)”).

parole.significato: metal (a chemical element that forms metallic bonds with other metals; usually shiny, malleable and hard)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”), from μέταλλευειν (métalleuein, “to mine, quarry”), of unknown origin, but apparently related to μέταλλαν (métallan, “to seek after”), also of unknown origin.

parole.significato: micro- (very small; 1/1,000,000)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μικρο- (mikro-).

parole.significato: monarchy (form of government in which sovereignty is embodied within a single, today usually hereditary head of state)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía), from μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”).

parole.significato: monarch (ruler of a monarchy)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”), from 'μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).

parole.significato: myth (ancient tale about gods, spirits, demons, heroes, natural phenomena or prehistoric events)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “word, humor, companion, speech, account, rumor, fable”).

parole.significato: neodymium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 60.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new, young”), and (di)dymium, a New Latin name given to a mixture of praseodymium and neodymium once thought to be one single chemical element.

parole.significato: neon (chemical element with atomic number 10, a noble gas, used in special light bulbs for advertising)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek νέον (néon), neuter of νέος (néos, “new”).

parole.significato: oligarchy (form of government run only by a few people)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía), from ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”).

parole.significato: osmium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 76.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”) (because of the strong smell of its oxide).

parole.significato: paleontology (science that studies the living organisms of past eras and their development, usually via their fossilize…
parole.testo: A new coinage, ultimately from Ancient Greek παλαιός (palaiós, “old”), ὤν (ṓn), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “to be”), and λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”) + -ija.

parole.significato: pathology
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos) and Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía).

parole.significato: politics (the branch of public activity, which includes the state system, administration, activity, relations between s…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek πολιτικά (politiká).

parole.significato: praseodymium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 59.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πράσιος (prásios, “leek-green”) and (di)dymium, a New Latin name given to a mixture of praseodymium and neodymium once thought to be one single chemical element.

parole.significato: prognosis
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek πρόγνωσις (prógnōsis, “foreknowledge, perceiving beforehand, prediction”), from προ- (pro-, “before”) + γνῶσις (gnôsis, “inquiry, investigation, knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”).

parole.significato: proto- (initial, first, original)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πρωτο- (prōto-), combining form of πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”), superlative of πρό (pró, “before”).

parole.significato: psyche (the human mind as the main force in thought, emotion, and behavior)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”), via some other European language (probably German).

parole.significato: psychiatry (branch of medicine that studies mental disorders, their causes, development, treatment and prevention)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) and ἰατρεία (iatreía, “healing, medical treatment”), from ἰατρός (iatrós, “doctor”).

parole.significato: rhodium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 45.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”), because of the colour of its salts' solutions.

parole.significato: rice (crop of the family Gramineae, esp. Oryza sativa)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), ὄρυζον (óruzon), itself a borrowing from Asian languages, probably ultimately from Dravidian, via Sanskrit व्रीहि (vrīhí). The specifics are still debated.

parole.significato: seismology (the study of vibrations of the Earth's interior, such as earthquakes)
parole.testo: A modern coinage, from Ancient Greek σεισμός (seismós, “earthquake”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).

parole.significato: symmetry
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).

parole.significato: symptom (an external sign of a disease or abnormal process)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a happening, accident, symptom of disease”), probably via some other European language.

parole.significato: scorpion (poisonous arachnids of the class Scorpiones)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos), probably via some other European language.

parole.significato: emerald
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek σμᾰ́ραγδος (smắragdos).

parole.significato: speleology, caving (the science that studies caves)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Ancient Greek σπήλαιον (spḗlaion, “cave”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, study”), with the suffix -ia (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: stomatology, dentistry (branch of medicine that studies the mouth and the oral cavity, their diseases, treatments, and…
parole.testo: A new coinage, ultimately from Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma, “mouth”) and -λογία (-logía, “study”).

parole.significato: thallium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 81.)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós, “green branch”), after the color of the radiation spectra.

parole.significato: technology
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek τεχνικός (tekhnikós).

parole.significato: technology
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek τεχνολογία (tekhnología).

parole.significato: technetium (radioactive metallic chemical element, with atomic number 43.)
parole.testo: From tehn- (“relating to technology”) (from Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē, “skill”)), because it was the first artificially created element.

parole.significato: theory
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría, “contemplation, speculation, a looking at, things looked at”), from θεωρέω (theōréō, “I look at, view, consider, examine”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”), from θέα (théa, “a view”) + ὁράω (horáō, “I see, look”).

parole.significato: therapy
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”), from θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “I serve, treat medically”).

parole.significato: thermos (flask with double walls between which there is a vacuum, used to keep something (usually food or liquid at a d…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Thermos, a trademarked name, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “warm”).

parole.significato: theater
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see", "to watch", "to observe”).

parole.significato: windpipe, airway, trachea (tube connecting the larynx to the lungs)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek τραχεῖα (trakheîa, “windpipe”), probably borrowed via another European language.

parole.significato: tragedy
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.

parole.significato: triphthong (sequence of three different vowels pronounced in one syllable)
parole.testo: A borrowing, via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek τρία (tría, “three”) and φθόγγος (phthóngos, “sound”).

parole.significato: telephone set, phone (electronic device used for communication between two people)
parole.testo: From tāls (“far”) + runa (“talk”), made into a masculine 2nd-declension noun (ending -is). Apparently a calque of German Fernsprecher, itself a calque of French téléphone, a word coined in the 1830s from two Ancient Greek elements, τῆλε (têle, “afar”) and φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice, sound”).

parole.significato: thulium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 69.)
parole.testo: From Thule, the name for the northernmost location of the ancient world (from Ancient Greek Θούλη (Thoúlē)), as a poetic way to say Scandinavia.

parole.significato: zoology (science that studies animalss, their structure, development, diversity and classification)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) and λόγος (lógos, “knowledge”) + -ija.

parole.significato: geophysics (science that studies the Earth's physical properties and the physical processes that occur in it)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek γῆ (gê, “earth”) and Latvian fizika (“physics”).

parole.significato: geography (the study of the physical structure and the inhabitants of the surface of the Earth)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) and γράφω (gráphō, “I write”) + -ija.

parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “I tear, split, cut”) + φρήν (phrḗn, “mind, brain, diaphragm”).
